title: Learning from Data: Models, Loss Functions and Risk

contract.reader: A programmer comfortable with calculus, linear algebra and elementary probability who is starting machine learning and wants its framing rather than a library tutorial
contract.problem: Understanding what a supervised learning problem is made of, what a good model means, and why the error on the training data is not the number that matters
contract.outcome: Define features, labels, model family, hypothesis class and loss; compare the common losses; define risk, Bayes risk, empirical risk and ERM; derive the conditional mean as the best squared-loss predictor; compute the exact risk of a fitted line on synthetic data and explain why training error is optimistic; state the held-out rule
contract.contribution: A synthetic example in which the risk is known exactly, so training error, Bayes risk and the fitted line's true risk sit side by side (0.1124, 0.2500, 0.2584), with a reproducible seeded script
contract.evidence: Derivations in the text; one NumPy script with quoted output; Bishop (2006); Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman (2009); James et al. (2013); Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014); Vapnik (1995)
contract.limitations: Supervised learning only; one feature and a linear model in the worked example; no generalization bounds; evaluation deferred to entry 4

findings.location: Section 3.2 decomposition display and Section 5.4 risk-of-the-fitted-line display (360 px; mobile-light-16, 25)
findings.problem: Both displays are cut at the right edge behind an unmarked scroll: the Var(y|x) term in 3.2, and the formula a^2 + ab + b^2/3 used to compute 0.2584 in 5.4, which appears nowhere else
findings.whyItMatters: These are the two results the argument rests on (the Bayes floor and the exact risk); a phone reader cannot follow or check the key computation
findings.action: Break both displays over lines (for example an aligned block with the right-hand side on its own line) so no line exceeds about 300 px
findings.acceptance: On new 360 px captures (light and dark) both displays are fully visible without sideways scrolling

findings.location: Section 2.2 linear-model display, Section 2.3 loss table, Section 5.1 data display (360 px; mobile-light-11, 12, 13, 21)
findings.problem: Loss table shows only Loss and Formula (cross-entropy formula cut, Task and Notes hidden); 2.2 display loses + w_d x_d; 5.1 display hides the noise distribution
findings.whyItMatters: The Notes column carries the comparison the table exists for
findings.action: Split the 2.2 and 5.1 displays; fold Task into the Loss cell so three columns fit, or add a site-level scroll cue
findings.acceptance: At 360 px the 2.2 and 5.1 displays are fully visible and the loss table Notes are visible, or a cue shows the table scrolls

findings.problem: The left-to-right Mermaid diagram keeps its minimum width; Predictions on new x is hidden to the right with no scroll cue
findings.whyItMatters: Small: the node the diagram leads to is the one a phone reader does not see
findings.action: Use flowchart TB for this diagram, or the site-level scroll cue for wide figures
findings.acceptance: At 360 px all six nodes are visible, or a visible cue shows that the figure scrolls

findings.location: Section 6 first paragraph and Section 5.4 excess-risk sentence
findings.problem: The page says the seed's training MSE fell well below its expectation and calls 0.0084 the price of estimation, without saying how typical the seed is; a 20,000-repetition simulation in review gives about 4% of samples at or below 0.1124 and a mean excess risk of about 0.027
findings.whyItMatters: The opening promises to say by how much results vary with the seed; readers may take the seeded numbers as typical
findings.action: Add one or two sentences giving the spread over repeated samples and the average excess risk from a stated, reproducible run; call 0.0084 this sample's excess risk
findings.acceptance: The live page states how typical the seed's training MSE and excess risk are, with numbers from a stated computation
